blocks.text:
Start here You’re playing tic-tac-toe. Can we build
a small electronic box that looks at the board and lights a red
LED if X has won? Before building anything, we must say exactly what the box should do. That exact description
is the first step of every circuit design.

Step 1: turn the problem
into 0s and 1s

blocks.caption:
Each square becomes one bit: 1 if it
has an X, 0 if not.

blocks.html:
• The board has 9 squares. Name them A₁₁, A₁₂, … A₃₃ (row, column).
  • For each square: Aᵢⱼ = 1 if it holds an X, 0 otherwise.
  • Rule: X wins if all three squares in any row, column or diagonal are 1.
  • Output W = 1 means “X has won” (red LED on).
blocks.text: The board has 9 squares. Name them A₁₁, A₁₂, … A₃₃ (row, column). For each square: Aᵢⱼ = 1 if it holds an X, 0 otherwise. Rule: X wins if all three squares in any row , column or diagonal are 1. Output W = 1 means “X has won” (red LED on).

blocks.html: Plain English (“X wins if they get three in a row”) can be unclear. Writing it in 0s and 1s makes it exact.

sections.title: Logic Gates — NOT, AND, OR and Friends

blocks.html: Start here A lift door should open only if the lift has stopped AND someone pressed the button. A fan should run if the switch is on OR the timer is on. A night lamp should glow when it is NOT bright outside. These three words, AND, OR and NOT, are the basic building blocks of every computer.
blocks.text:
Start here A lift door should open only if the lift has stopped AND someone pressed the button . A
fan should run if the switch is on OR the timer is on .
A night lamp should glow when it is NOT bright outside.
These three words, AND, OR and NOT, are the basic building blocks of
every computer.
The three basic gates

blocks.caption:
Each gate’s symbol, its rule, and its full
truth table.

blocks.html:
Gate Written as Read as Output is 1 when…
NOT A̅ (or A′) “not A” A is 0 (it flips the input)
AND A · B (or AB) “A and B” both A and B are 1
OR A + B “A or B” at least one of A, B is 1
blocks.text: Gate Written as Read as Output is 1 when… NOT A̅ (or A′) “not A” A is 0 (it flips the input) AND A · B (or AB) “A and B” both A and B are 1 OR A + B “A or B” at least one of A, B is 1

Two useful facts (they come up a lot):

blocks.html:
• XOR with many inputs = 1 when an odd number of inputs are 1.
  • XNOR of two inputs = 1 when A = B. That’s a 1-bit comparator.

Order of operations
(precedence)

blocks.html: What does W · X̅ + Y · Z mean? Just like × before + in normal maths:

1. NOT first (highest)
  2. then AND
  3. then OR (lowest)

blocks.html: Start here In school maths, you learned rules like a × 1 = a and a + 0 = a. They let you simplify long expressions. Boolean algebra has its own rules for 0s and 1s. A simpler expression means fewer gates, so a cheaper, faster, cooler chip.
blocks.text:
Start here In school maths, you learned rules like a
× 1 = a and a + 0 = a. They let you simplify long expressions. Boolean
algebra has its own rules for 0s and 1s. A simpler expression means fewer gates , so a cheaper, faster,
cooler chip.
Where the rules come from

blocks.html:
• Axioms: basic facts we accept as true at the start (like “0 ≠ 1”).
  • Laws and theorems: rules we prove from the axioms, and then use to simplify.
blocks.text:
Axioms: basic facts we accept as true at the start
(like “0 ≠ 1”). Laws and theorems: rules we prove from the axioms, and then use to simplify.
The laws (with their “duals”)

blocks.html: Every law comes in a pair. In the second one (the dual), AND ↔︎ OR and 0 ↔︎ 1 are swapped.
blocks.text: Every law comes in a pair . In the second one (the dual ), AND ↔︎ OR and 0 ↔︎ 1 are swapped.

blocks.caption:
Each law and its dual: swap AND with OR, and
0 with 1.

blocks.html:
Law OR version AND version (dual) In words
Identity X + 0 = X X · 1 = X 0 doesn’t change an OR; 1 doesn’t change an AND
Null (domination) X + 1 = 1 X · 0 = 0 OR with 1 is always 1; AND with 0 is always 0
Idempotent X + X = X X · X = X Repeating doesn’t change anything
Involution (X̅)̅ = X Flip twice = original
Complement X + X̅ = 1 X · X̅ = 0 Something OR its opposite = 1; AND = 0
Commutative X + Y = Y + X X · Y = Y · X Order doesn’t matter
Associative (X + Y) + Z = X + (Y + Z) (X · Y) · Z = X · (Y · Z) Brackets don’t matter
Distributive X · (Y + Z) = XY + XZ X + Y·Z = (X + Y)(X + Z) The second one is new! It doesn’t work in normal maths

The two laws

blocks.caption:
A NOR gate does the same job as
an AND gate with both inputs flipped. A NAND gate does the same job as
an OR gate with both inputs flipped.

2 (A · B)̅ = A̅ + B̅ NOT (A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B)

around

blocks.text: Big ideas

blocks.html:
• First write a functional specification (what output for each input) and a timing specification (how fast).
  • Combinational logic has no memory; sequential logic remembers (from Week 7).
  • A truth table has 2ⁿ rows. It gets huge fast, so we use Boolean algebra.
  • Gates: NOT (flip), AND (all 1), OR (any 1), NAND, NOR, XOR (different / odd number of 1s), XNOR (same).
  • Precedence: NOT → AND → OR.
  • Laws come in dual pairs (swap + ↔︎ ·, 0 ↔︎ 1). Shortcuts: XY + XY̅ = X, X + XY = X, X + YZ = (X + Y)(X + Z).
  • De Morgan: (A + B)̅ = A̅B̅ and (AB)̅ = A̅ + B̅. NOR = AND with flipped inputs; NAND = OR with flipped inputs.
  • SOP: for each row with F = 1, write a minterm (1 → letter, 0 → barred letter) and OR them. Short form Σm(…).
